prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B010 to a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks. The reasons are scientific and I would give the same ones if the count were different. The decisive idea, a lattice at the magic wavelength that cancels the differential light shift so that thousands of atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free, is separable from both the frequency comb and ion-trap control. The result is quantitatively understood: blackbody, higher-order lattice and collisional shifts are controlled by theory that matches measurement. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced in independent laboratories and compared across continents, and that is the test of robustness I apply to any result, including my own field's. The credit follows the record: Katori for the proposal and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the frontier and for the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock. A two-name citation is therefore faithful and fits inside the three-person limit with room to spare. I would word the citation around the lattice clock itself, so that the comb and the ion clocks remain preconditions and not the subject.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks is real, and I defer to my atomic-physics colleagues on whether the lattice clock is a distinct enough step. Part of the payoff is still prospective because the SI second has not been redefined. Tests of constants have so far given null results, so the case rests on a new regime of measurement capability and not on a surprise in nature. Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and others fall outside two names, and a hard boundary at two is a genuine cost. Finally, I give up what I still regard as the most attractive condensed-matter story on the list, the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction answered by the 2018 experiments. I do not withdraw its scientific merit; I judge it not yet ready, since the pairing mechanism is unresolved, Yuan Cao is outside the trio, and the field is about eight years old.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the frequency comb only counts optical cycles and does not contain the idea of trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and says B010 should wait one more cycle while the settled lattice clock goes first.
responses.response: That distinction is what moved me. The comb is the readout and the magic-wavelength lattice is the thing that makes the atomic reference accurate, so a citation naming the lattice makes the subject separable from 2005. I also accept your point about Cao: he is first author of the decisive 2018 papers, and no wording of a three-name prize fixes it, whereas for B004 nobody has shown a missing decisive third name. I disagree with you on one point, namely that the clock tests of constants and redshift are the reason to prefer B004. Those results are null or demonstration-level so far, and I would defend the prize on capability and on independent reproducibility.

responses.point: Lindroth asks the committee to be comfortable with the superconductivity question before honouring B010, and would justify B004 by capability, noting that a measurement tool is less of a surprise in nature.
responses.response: I agree and I now accept your condition, since I cannot say the pairing mechanism is settled. In round 1 I asked you whether the 2005 overlap was resolved. Your own description of the lattice clock as a clean piece of atomic-structure physics (choosing the wavelength where the light shift cancels) persuades me it is an invention and not just a refinement. I share your unease about rewarding a tool more than a surprise, and I think the citation should say so honestly, by naming the invention and the 10^-18 performance and not claiming a discovery of new physics.

responses.point: Pearce asked me whether the interpretation of B010 is settled enough, and said he would not want B010 crowded out only because it has five names under three slots.
responses.response: My answer is that it is not settled for the pairing physics, and I would not ask the committee to pretend otherwise. The phenomenology is firmly reproduced, but the interpretation is moving, which is where B004 is stronger. I agree that the five-name problem is not a reason to dismiss B010, and I keep it as my first alternative so it is not penalised for the three-seat limit. A two-part prize combining B004 with B010 would need more than three people, since B004 already uses two, so I do not propose one.

responses.point: Olsson says she cannot settle whether Katori's proposal or the first operational clock marks the original contribution, and that B010 is the better-structured alternative if credit cannot be apportioned to two people.
responses.response: On B004 the proposal and the first operational strontium clock are both Katori's, so the question is whether the decisive demonstrations then belong to Ye. As a non-specialist I read the record as two identifiable contributions, concept and first realisation, then accuracy records and the many-body clock, which supports two names. I agree with your fallback logic: if an AMO colleague can show a decisive third contribution, I would reconsider, and B010 would then be the better-structured option. No one has shown that yet.

responses.point: Kroll sees the technique as having already enabled other work and stresses that the Katori and Ye attribution is unusually tidy and faithful to the record.
responses.response: I accept the attribution argument, and it answers the chair's question about two names for me. I would add one caution from my own side: the reproducibility that I value, independent groups agreeing at the 1e-18 level, is about uncertainty budgets, so I would ask AMO colleagues to confirm that the comparisons across RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB and SYRTE are truly independent and not one lineage of design choices. If that holds, it is the strongest reproducibility case on the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I defer to AMO colleagues and would reconsider if they split on this.
Whether two names fairly cover the record given Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and the SYRTE group.
Whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition; I lean to proceeding on performance and reproduction.
Whether B010 will look stronger in a later cycle once the pairing mechanism and the attribution around Cao are clearer.
How far my own shift from B010 reflects the strength of the B004 argument rather than the pull of a seven-to-one count; I have tried to test it on the physics.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed. I work at Uppsala in theoretical magnetism and DFT and have no stated collaboration with Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. My only field-proximity interest remains B027 (DFT+DMFT), which I am not preferring. I note that I held B010 as my round-1 first choice and moving away from it is not a conflict. No recusal is needed on B004 on my side.
